title: 1974: the alimony judge who heard him play at his house
summary: Howard tells how a judge in his divorce case recognised him from playing at the judge's house and set alimony at a dollar a week.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Meeting, courting and marrying: musicians' love lives

blocks.x: Oh, yes, he got a few jobs. The last time -- now, this is -- you'll have to take this out, because I don't want my wife to find it out, but I'll tell you two.

My first wife got a divorce from me, and we were -- she's here right now, living right in town. And you know where she was? I was out there to the judge's where we played with Mac, the night before I had to go down there that day, and she had about eight or nine women up there against me, you know, against me as -- you know.

Witnesses, yeah. Eight or nine of them. And they was raising hell. And I'll think of the judge's name pretty soon. But he looked down there and said, "Hey you, come here." That's just the way he said it. I walked up there and I was scared to death. He said, "Weren't you out to my house last night with Mr. Howdy McVey?" That's what they called him, Howdy McVey. I said, "Yes, I was. I played at your house last night." "You play all that good music and you've got all these people here? What are you doing? What are you doing?" "I'm not doing nothing. I didn't do nothing." My wife said I didn't want to pay her alimony. I gave her some money but that wasn't enough. "How much you give her?" "Well, I only make around 10 or $12.00 a week." He said, "How much you --" (Unintelligible). That's all I was making at Bullock's. I was head janitor there. And and forget it you know, he says, "You pay her $1.00 a week and go home and
forget it. Get out of here. Get out of the courtroom." Well, boy, that never got out of this town. Lots of people --
